title: About 70% of the land that burns on Earth each year is in Africa
body: More fires burn in Africa each year than anywhere else on Earth, and NASA satellite data put them at **70% of the area burned** worldwide. Most are set on purpose, by people burning land for farming and grazing: fire clears old vegetation, opens new ground to plant and returns nutrients to the soil. The burning follows the dry season, so a wave of fire sweeps across the savannas just south of the Sahara, then shifts to the south of the continent half a year later. Every year Africa's fires burn an area [about half the size of the continental United States](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/researchers-detect-a-global-drop-in-fires-90493/).

slides.heading: Of all the area burned by fire worldwide, the share in Africa
slides.note: NASA estimate from satellite fire observations, 2002 to 2011

slides.heading: Fire on purpose
slides.text: People set most of Africa's fires, a practice widespread and accepted by the continent's fire managers. Lightning starts far fewer, mostly at the start of the wet season, when it strikes vegetation that is still dry.

slides.label: drop in the area burned worldwide between 1998 and 2015
slides.text: The fall was biggest in savannas and grasslands, as people moved to permanent fields and villages. Africa's savanna fires shrank by 700,000 km².

slides.question: Why does Africa's band of fires move from north to south of the equator and back?
slides.explanation: Burning spreads as the dry season progresses, and the dry season comes at opposite times of year on either side of the equator.
